subject: Dedicated capacity: topology + burst characteristics for NexaHealth
messages:
From: Alex Turner <alex.turner@nexahealth.com>
To: marissa.cole@redwood.com
Date: 2028-08-20T16:12:00Z
Subject: Topology & burst characteristics for Dedicated sizing

Hey Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo last week — NexaHealth is moving quickly and we want to make sure we size Dedicated correctly before we commit. I attached a quick workload snapshot (nexa_workload_snapshot.csv) with hourly qps and a short sample of API traces. High-level details below: 

- Product: Virtual clinical assistant (chat-first) + short retrieval requests.
- Daily active users (DAU): ~200k.
- Typical concurrent users (sustained): 2.8k - 3.5k during business hours.
- Peak burst: observed up to ~12k concurrent for 2-5 minute windows on promotional days. This is a recurring pattern (roughly 3x/month).
- Prompt length (user input): median ~140 tokens, 90th ~320.
- Response length (generated): median ~180 tokens, 90th ~420.
- Mix: ~70% conversational (multi-turn sessions with session affinity), ~30% stateless retrieval/generation.
- Streaming: we use token streaming for UX; about 85% of generation calls are streamed.
- P50 latency target for responses: 350ms; p95 target: 900ms (for 99% of requests we expect fallbacks to maintain <1.5s).

Questions for Redwood:
1) What topology (GPU SKUs + per-GPU concurrency assumptions) would you provision for steady-state vs peak bursts?
2) How would you handle the short, high-amplitude bursts (12k concurrent) without overprovisioning?
3) Any caching/batching/quantization guidance for our prompt/response mix?

We can share deeper traces if needed.

Thanks — looking to get a preliminary sizing + options by end of week so we can feed into procurement.

— Alex
Alex Turner
Director of Platform, NexaHealth
alex.turner@nexahealth.com

Alex — great data, thanks. A few clarifying questions so our pre-sales sizing is aligned to your traffic model: 

1) Session affinity: when you say multi-turn sessions, do you expect affinity for the entire user session (typical session lengths / number of requests per session)?
2) Streaming behavior: are streams long-lived (lots of tokens streamed over >1s) or short bursts (final response arrives within 500ms)?
3) Retry/failure model: do you have client-side retries that could multiply load during partial outages?
4) Multi-region: do you require active-active across US regions or are you okay with single-region footprint + DR?
5) Off-peak sustained QPS: what's the 03:00–05:00 local sustained QPS baseline (helps size steady-state pool).

If you can get us the p50/p95 per-endpoint from the traces (or let us run a short stress test pointing at a staging endpoint), we can produce a realistic GPU map (SKUs, model parallelism, quantization tradeoffs) and an autoscaling policy that targets your p95 SLO while limiting committed capacity.

I attached our short preflight checklist — the team likes to use that as the shared intake.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwood.com

Attachments: redwood_dedicated_preflight.pdf
From: Alex Turner <alex.turner@nexahealth.com>
To: marissa.cole@redwood.com
Date: 2028-08-21T09:14:00Z
Subject: Re: Topology & burst characteristics for Dedicated sizing

Marissa — quick answers inline: 

1) Session affinity: yes, we pin sessions to the same session-id for the duration. Typical session has 3–6 turns, median ~4 requests. Session duration median ~45s.
2) Streaming: responses are token-streamed; about 60% of streams finish within 400–600ms, 30% are 600–1500ms, and ~10% stream longer (especially long clinical summaries).
3) Retries: client retries are conservative (up to 2 retries with exponential backoff). We do see amplification risk during partial outages.
4) Regions: US-East primary; we want a small US-West active standby (warm), not full active-active.
5) Off-peak QPS (03:00–05:00 PST): sustained ~220 QPS, burst windows still happen from promotional campaigns.

I'm attaching a zip with a few sample traces (nexa_api_traces.zip) and a short token distribution histogram. Let me know if you'd like us to run a dedicated staging stress-target.

— Alex

Quick take — I'll draft a one-pager but here are starting assumptions and immediate asks: 

Assumptions:
- Target model: open-architecture LLM tuned for clinical summarization; baseline inference cost assumes 16-bit (fp16) quantized variant for steady-state and an int8-ish variant for aggressive burst compacting if acceptable on quality.
- Per-GPU steady concurrency: 100–140 effective requests/s (streaming reduces effective throughput; assume 30% lower throughput when majority are streaming).
- Steady-state (3.5k concurrent): ~26–35 GPUs (NVIDIA L-series equivalent) with KV cache enabled and batching tuned for average 180-token response.
- Burst guard (handle 12k concurrent): layered approach — reserved baseline + autoscaler with burst buffer (warm standby nodes + cheap overflow fallbacks):~ baseline reserve 35 GPUs + 120 transient burst GPUs that can spin up in 60–120s, plus a policy to offload low-priority retrieval to smaller models.

Immediate asks to finalize numbers:
1) Provide p50/p95 observed latency from the traces for the top 3 endpoints (so we can validate the per-GPU latency curves).
2) Confirm SLO hard limits for critical flows — above we used p95 = 900ms as target.
3) Any client-side batching/windowing we can instrument to flatten spikes? (even small client-side jitter reduces peak amplitude).

Notes: we should recommend a canary where we enable an int8 variant that reduces GPU footprint by ~30–40% for non-critical requests with rigorous evals on quality. Rishi, can you sketch estimated quality deltas for int8 vs fp16 on their sample traces?

I'll assemble the two capacity options (minimal committed + aggressive reserved + transient burst plan) and cost ballparks today and share a one-page.

— Karthik
Principal Infra Planner, Redwood Inference
